2. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 contested the suit by filing separate written statements. Defendant No. 2 denied to have acted as agent of defendant No. 1. Its contention is that the suit is barred by limitation and is bad for non- joinder of necessary parties. It has been further asserted that defendant No. 2 did not extend the period of limitation nor did it acknowledge the liability; that the plaintiff lodged the claim within time with regard to short landing of 6 drums in another consignment in the same shipment and hence the payment was made, but there was no inducement or fraud on the part of defendant No. 2 that the disputed claim would be satisfied. 

 4. Is the suit bad for non-joinder of parties? 

 Issue No. 1: In Admiralty Suit No. 14 of 1980 to which the present plaintiff and defendant No. 3 were parties, it was decided that a suit for compensation for non delivery of goods carried in a ship is maintainable under the Admiralty Jurisdiction of this Court. In that case it was also decided that the plaintiff, a nationalised concern under the supervision and control of the B.C.l.C under the President's Order No. 27 of 1972 had the locus standi to file a suit, for compensation for short landing of goods, on its own. 

 The short landing of 25 drums of the cargo is not disputed. On behalf of defendant No. 2 it has been contended that the owner of the ship AYUTHIA, though a necessary party has not been impleaded and so the suit is bad for non-joinder of parties and it must fail Relying on Ext. A the cargo of M.S. AYUTHIA (wrongly stated as S.S. AYUTHIA in the plaint), Ext. B cargo manifest, Ext. D letter dated 21.7.80 from defendant No. 2 to the plaintiff, Ext. E letter dated 22.10.80 from defendant No. 2 to the plaintiff, Ext. F photostat copy of letter dated 9.7.80 from the East Asiatic Company to defendant No. 2 it has been urged that defendant No. 2 is the agent of the East Asiatic Company Limited which has not been impleaded in the' suit. Defendant No. 2 filed an application on 28.4.82 for bringing on record the time charter dated 2nd August, 1978 between, Esolanade Maritime Inc. of Liberia, the owner of M.S. AYUTHIA and East Asiatic Company Limited, the Charterers. It has been contended by the defendant that defendant No. 1 is in no way connected with the disputed matter and that defendant No. 2, acting as agent of the East Asiatic Company Limited, ought to have been impleaded in the suit along with the owners of the ship. 

 4. It has been conceded by the plaintiff that defendant No. 1 is not a proper party in the suit, but as defendant No. 2 filed a suit for declaration under section 55(1) (e) of the Customs Act, 1969 and as he did Dot disclose the name of the owners of the ship and as D.W. 1 admitted that ultimate responsibilities for the loss of the plaintiff's cargo was to be borne by the owners, presence of defendant No. 2 is sufficient, for adjudication of the matter and absence of the owners of the ship or of the charterers would not non-suit the plaintiff. 

 5. It is nobody's case that defendant No. 2 entered into an agreement on behalf of the owners of the ship or the charterers. Section 64(d) of the Sea Customs Act, 1878 which is similar to 55(1)(e) of the Customs Act, 1969 came the for consideration in Sea farers Ine. Vs. Province of East Pakistan 20 D.L.R. S.C. 225. The Supreme Court observed: "It will be seen that these provisions create a statutory liability on a shipping agent on the basis of the declaration delivered by him to the Customs Collector, to discharge all claims for damages or short delivery which may be established in respect of goods comprised in the import cargo. He incurs this statutory liability as an agent on behalf of his master, the principal. His entity is thus linked up with that of the principal without whom it is non-existent."
